lessons.title: DNA structure and replication
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Biology — Nucleic acids; DNA replication; protein synthesis (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the structure of a nucleotide and of the DNA double helix.
Apply complementary base pairing and Chargaff's rules.
Explain semi-conservative replication and the roles of the enzymes.
reviewNotes: Direction labels 3′/5′ are standard; check how much detail is expected.
Uses ¹⁵N / ¹⁴N and Meselson–Stahl results as a standard textbook description.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Nucleotides and the double helix
blocks.md: A **nucleotide** has a pentose sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA), a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. Nucleotides join by **phosphodiester bonds** (condensation) into a sugar-phosphate backbone. DNA is a **double helix** of two **antiparallel** strands held by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: **A–T** (two bonds) and **G–C** (three bonds). The bases are A, T, G, C; RNA has **uracil (U)** instead of T.

blocks.title: Purines and pyrimidines; RNA vs DNA
blocks.md: **Purines** (A, G) have two rings; **pyrimidines** (C, T, U) have one ring. A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, so the helix has constant width. DNA is double-stranded, with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is usually single-stranded with ribose and uracil. In DNA the amount of A equals T and the amount of G equals C (**Chargaff's rule**); this is not true for single-stranded RNA.

items.text: DNA: two antiparallel strands, complementary bases

blocks.caption: DNA ladder model: sugar-phosphate backbones and complementary base pairs joined by hydrogen bonds.
blocks.alt: Two vertical blue backbones joined by four dashed red rungs labelled with base pairs A-T, G-C, T-A, C-G.

blocks.title: Semi-conservative replication
blocks.md:
1. **Helicase** unwinds and breaks hydrogen bonds between bases.
2. Each strand is a template; free nucleotides pair by complementary bases.
3. **DNA polymerase** joins nucleotides, always at the 3′ end (so the leading strand is continuous and the lagging strand is made in short **Okazaki fragments**).
4. **DNA ligase** joins fragments. Each new DNA molecule has one old and one new strand.

blocks.title: Evidence
blocks.md: In the **Meselson–Stahl** experiment bacteria grown in heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) were moved to light nitrogen (¹⁴N). After one generation all DNA was of intermediate density, after two generations half intermediate and half light. This fits the semi-conservative model and rules out the conservative one.

blocks.title: Worked example — base proportions
blocks.statement: A DNA sample contains 28 % adenine. Work out the percentage of each of the other bases.
steps: A = T, so thymine is also 28 %.

blocks.title: Worked example — replication and 15N
blocks.statement: A DNA molecule with both strands labelled ¹⁵N replicates three times in ¹⁴N medium. What fraction of the molecules contain any ¹⁵N?
steps: After 3 rounds there are 2³ = 8 DNA molecules.
The two original ¹⁵N strands end up in only two molecules.

lessons.title: Protein synthesis and gene mutations
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Biology — Nucleic acids; DNA replication; protein synthesis (to be checked)

objectives: Use the genetic code to work out mRNA and amino-acid sequences.
Explain the effects of gene mutations such as the sickle-cell substitution.
reviewNotes: Codon assignments used (AUG Met, GCU Ala, UUU Phe, GAA Glu, UGG Trp, stop codons) are standard; the question set uses given codons.
Sickle-cell: Glu to Val at position 6 of the β-globin chain is standard; the position is not stated in the text.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: From gene to protein
blocks.md: A **gene** is a sequence of DNA bases coding for a polypeptide. In **transcription** RNA polymerase makes a single-stranded **mRNA** copy of the **template strand**, using complementary bases (A pairs with U). In eukaryotes the primary transcript is **spliced**: non-coding **introns** are removed and **exons** joined. mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore.

blocks.title: Codons, anticodons and the template strand
blocks.md: A **codon** is three bases on mRNA; an **anticodon** is the complementary three bases on tRNA. The mRNA has the same sequence as the *coding* (non-template) strand, with U for T. So if the template is TAC the mRNA codon is AUG and the tRNA anticodon is UAC. Always write the three types clearly and say which strand you are reading.

blocks.caption: Genetic information flows from DNA to mRNA (transcription) to a polypeptide (translation).
blocks.alt: Three boxes joined by arrows: DNA, mRNA and polypeptide, labelled transcription and translation.

blocks.title: Translation
blocks.md: The mRNA binds to a **ribosome** (rRNA and protein). Each **tRNA** carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon. The ribosome holds two tRNAs at a time, and a **peptide bond** forms between their amino acids. The ribosome moves along the mRNA codon by codon from the start codon **AUG** until a **stop codon** (UAA, UAG, UGA) is reached.

blocks.title: Properties of the code and mutations
blocks.md: The code is a **triplet** code, **degenerate** (several codons per amino acid), **non-overlapping** and almost **universal**. **Substitution** can be silent, missense or nonsense. **Insertion or deletion** of bases shifts the reading frame (frameshift). In sickle-cell disease a single substitution in the haemoglobin β-chain gene changes glutamic acid to valine, so haemoglobin S forms fibres in low oxygen.

blocks.title: Worked example — gene to polypeptide
blocks.statement: The template strand reads TAC CGA AAA. Use these codons: AUG = Met, GCU = Ala, UUU = Phe. Give the mRNA and the amino acids.
steps: Complementary bases (T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C): TAC → AUG; CGA → GCU; AAA → UUU.
Read the codons: Met – Ala – Phe.

blocks.title: Worked example — counting codons
blocks.statement: A coding region of an mRNA is 150 bases long and ends with a stop codon. How many amino acids does the polypeptide contain?
steps: The last codon is a stop codon and does not code for an amino acid.
